newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - British Museum cashes in on money.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - British Museum cashes in on money.

text.p: The British Museum is cashing in on cash with the world's first gallery devoted to money.
Money has made the world go round for centuries and the coin curator at London's most famous museum believes the credit card hasn't killed cash off just yet.
"At the end of this millennium it might seem that money as we know it is on the way out," said curator Virginia Hewitt.
"The gallery is an invitation to take a fresh look at where money came from and where it's going."
Coins and paper, poverty and riches, vice and virtue -- money has always been more to humans than just a means of exchanging financial obligations. To many, it is the root of all evil.

To underline money's diverse history, the gallery is divided into three sections, spanning the earliest known monetary systems in the third millennium BC in Mesopotamia, Egypt and China to the growing use of plastic payment cards at the end of the 20th century and the planned single currency for Europe.

Of the museum's collection of about one million money-related exhibits, around 5,000 are on display. The exhibition features the different forms of money, its manipulation by governments and individuals, and the way it has been used throughout the millennia.
"The gallery looks at the use of money across societies in a universal way to show the similarities and differences between different cultures," said Hewitt.
VAST AND VARIED COLLECTION
The collection encompasses a wealth of ancient and mediaeval coins but also displays 20th century items such as washing machine tokens, cheque books, telephone cards and travellers cheques.
"Curious money", such as stones, pieces of wood, copper rings and feathers, was widely described by European travellers from the 15th century, highlighting money's cultural diversity.
The use of money boxes is another way of displaying the different cultural influences on money, said Hewitt.

A prayer-book shaped money box, issued by the Midland Bank in the 1930s, counsels the moral propriety of thrift, whereas a modern-day money box made in Burma in the 1990s is shaped like a television set.
Will the bronze pfennig stuck into a plastic money pig, made in Germany in 1991, soon be replaced by the euro, Europe's planned single currency?

The first part of the gallery spans from 2500 BC to about AD 600. It covers the period from the earliest records of payments in grain or metal in ancient Mesopotamia, to the beginnings of coinage in the late seventh century BC and its widespread adoption through much of the ancient world.
The second covers a millennium to AD 1700. During that period coinage remained the main form of money as we know it.

In Europe, the Islamic world and south Asia, gold and silver coins predominated, whereas in east Asia, coinage was made only in bronze, supplemented by other forms of money such as paper which was first used in China during the 11th century.

The discovery of the Americas and the exploitation of their mineral wealth saw the introduction there of European forms of coinage, leading to the emergence of a global economy and coins circulating around the world.

The 20th century has seen the greatest changes. At the end of this millennium, the use of credit cards, first used in the United States in 1946 and introduced in Europe 20 years later, is accelerating.
A long way from Mesopotamia, or the coins of ancient Rome, when goddess Juno Moneda gave money its name.

But the common use of "plastic money", predominantly in the western world, cannot be taken for granted everywhere. In many countries, credit card use is not as widespread as in Britain or the United States.
"Not even access to a bank account is available to everyone everywhere, so to think paper money and coins will disappear in the foreseeable future might be a bit premature," said Hewitt.
And as many new nations appear on the world map, such as in the former Soviet Union, new banknotes appear and are being printed at a rapid place, she said.
